analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to knowingly put people in danger of death by violating environmental laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have imposed up to 15 years in prison and a $1 million fine on companies and individuals who knowingly endanger people through environmental violations, was introduced in June 1992 with no cosponsors, got one subcommittee hearing, and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new federal crime: knowingly exposing another person to imminent danger of death or serious injury through a violation of major environmental laws like hazardous waste and drinking water rules [S3]. An individual could face up to 15 years in prison, a corporation up to a $1 million fine, with penalties doubled for repeat offenses [S3]. Courts would also be required to bar federal agencies from signing contracts with, or making loans or grants to, a convicted violator for the facility where the crime happened, until the EPA certifies the problem is fixed [S3]. Convicted organizations would be put on probation and forced to pay for an independent environmental audit of their operations [S3], and people whose tips lead to a conviction could receive rewards of up to $10,000 [S3]. The bill never got past the House Judiciary Committee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and residents who live near polluting facilities. The bill creates a serious personal criminal penalty for company officials and companies that knowingly put people in imminent danger of death or serious bodily injury through violations of hazardous waste, drinking water, pesticide, ocean dumping, toxics, and community right-to-know laws [S3]. It also gives neighbors and workers a financial incentive to report such crimes, with rewards up to $10,000 for tips that lead to conviction [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and residents near polluting facilities

how_it_helps.text: Makes knowingly endangering someone's life through an environmental violation a federal crime punishable by up to 15 years in prison for individuals and a $1 million fine for corporations, doubled for repeat offenders [S3].

Bars federal agencies from contracting with, or lending or granting money to, a convicted violator for the facility where the offense occurred until the EPA certifies the dangerous condition is corrected [S3].
Requires convicted organizations to serve probation and pay for an independent court-appointed expert to audit their operations and recommend fixes the court can order them to implement [S3].
Authorizes rewards of up to $10,000 for private citizens whose information leads to a conviction for these environmental crimes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies and their executives that violate environmental laws in ways that knowingly endanger people, plus hazardous waste handlers, chemical plants, and other regulated facilities facing criminal exposure and court-ordered audits they must pay for [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill grants broad criminal immunity for violations discovered during a court-ordered audit: a company, its officers, and employees cannot be criminally prosecuted for environmental violations found in the audit unless they failed to cooperate with it or comply with the court's order [S3]. Critics could argue this turns the remedy for serious wrongdoing into a shield.

The knowledge standard is demanding: a defendant is liable only for actual personal awareness that the conduct endangered someone, and knowledge held by others in the company cannot be attributed to them, though prosecutors may use circumstantial evidence of steps taken to stay ignorant [S3]. That makes convictions hard to obtain against top executives.

The President may exempt any contract, loan, or grant from the contractor ban if deemed necessary to the paramount interest of the United States, a broad escape valve [S3]. The bill also had no cosponsors, suggesting the environmental or legal community had not rallied behind this particular design [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — treating deliberate endangerment of people through pollution as a serious crime rather than a paperwork violation — directly serves public safety, and the contractor ban and audit requirements add real teeth. But the bill contains significant carve-outs: a demanding actual-knowledge standard, an affirmative defense where the endangered person consented, a presidential exemption, and immunity for violations surfaced in the audit process. As written it was a modest tightening, not a sweeping crackdown, and it attracted no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to its crime subcommittee; the subcommittee held one hearing and then the bill sat until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993, never reaching a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on June 2, 1992, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On June 5, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, which held a hearing on June 11, 1992 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never left committee and never received a vote in the House or Senate before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and individuals whose environmental violations put people in danger are better off, because the bill's criminal penalties, contractor ban, and mandatory audits never became law. The House Judiciary Committee also avoided taking any position on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that knowingly endanger people through pollution

against.name: House Committee on Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 2, 1992, referred it to the crime subcommittee, and never reported it out for a floor vote

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors, and no vote was ever recorded, so no party split is visible in the record [S1, S4].

industries.industry: Hazardous waste handlers and polluting industrial facilities
industries.note: The bill would have exposed company officers and organizations to up to 15 years' imprisonment and $1 million fines for knowingly endangering people through waste, water, and toxics violations, and forced convicted companies to pay for independent compliance audits [S3]. Its death left those facilities facing only the pre-existing penalty structure.
A convicted violator would have been barred from federal contracts, loans, and grants for the facility where the crime occurred until the EPA certified a fix [S3]. This penalty never took effect.
